rag_semantic_descriptions: Slowloris is holding hundreds of connections open to the web server by sending partial HTTP requests that never include the final blank line needed to complete the header block.
The attacker intentionally withholds the terminating CRLF sequence from each HTTP request, causing the server to keep every connection thread alive waiting for a request that will never finish.
Periodically, the tool sends fake additional headers like 'X-a: b' at extremely slow intervals to reset the server's idle connection timer and prevent timeout-based disconnection.
This low-and-slow attack consumes nearly zero bandwidth but is devastating to thread-based web servers like older Apache versions, where each held connection permanently blocks a worker thread.
The flow data reveals extremely long-lived sessions with tiny packet sizes and massive inter-arrival times — the attacker sends just enough data to keep the connection from being dropped.
Because each connection completes a valid TCP three-way handshake and uses standard HTTP syntax, volumetric DDoS protection appliances see nothing abnormal at the network layer.
The server's thread pool is being slowly starved as Slowloris opens new connections faster than old ones expire, eventually leaving no worker threads available for legitimate visitors.
Each individual Slowloris connection looks like a single slow client, but the pattern of many simultaneous never-completing requests from the same source or coordinated sources reveals the attack.
The micro-packet sizing is distinctive — the attacker sends only a few bytes of text every few seconds, just enough to constitute a valid but incomplete HTTP header line.
This attack is particularly effective because a single attacker with minimal resources can bring down a web server that doesn't implement connection timeouts or per-client connection limits.
